title: The Longreads Questionnaire, Featuring Roberto José Andrade Franco
author: Longreads
content:
Four years ago, I read Roberto José Andrade Franco’s ESPN story about Tess Mata, one of the students killed in the Robb Elementary School shooting in Uvalde, and I’ve never forgotten an image in it: a determined Tess outside in the Texas heat, aiming her softball pitches at a target on a tree in her family’s yard. That’s what Franco does so well. He creates moments that linger—about sports, Texas, loss, and identity and in-betweenness—and makes me care about the people he puts on the page.

Franco grew up on the El Paso-Juárez border. In a 2020 National Magazine Award-nominated essay that he wrote one year after the El Paso massacre, he reflects on the lifelong pull to this paradox of a place: “It’s where things make the most sense. Where it’s easy to love, even if it’s difficult to live.” I love that he writes from this borderland even when he’s somewhere else. During Mexico’s first World Cup match earlier this summer, he was in Woodburn, Oregon, a small town where Latinos make up more than 60 percent of the population and own nearly every business downtown. Residents had been shaken by last fall’s ICE raids, but they showed up to watch and celebrate. There, thousands of miles from El Paso, Franco found something familiar: a hardworking, resilient community with deep Latino roots and a fierce sense of pride.

I also credit Franco with piquing my interest in wrestling stories, including his piece on WWW star Eddie Guerrero, which also explores family and legacy. Whether he’s writing about sports heroes or ordinary people, or tracing the history of Texas or his own, Franco never fails to move me.

Below, he explains why enrolling in community college at 28 was the most meaningful journey he’s taken, tells us his favorite meal (and the ideal season to eat it), and recognizes a fellow sports writer who inspires him. When asked to name three publications he enjoys reading, he gives a shout-out to Texas Highways, a magazine we love—and it just so happens that he’s the guest editor of its October 2026 issue, focused on El Paso. After spending time with Franco here, read his feature on the city’s historic Smelter Cemetery, and then explore the rest of the magazine.

—Cheri Lucas Rowlands

Where did you grow up?

Several places, but mostly on the El Paso-Juárez border. 

I was born in Chicago, but we lived in Juárez, Mexico, until I was about 6. Then we moved across the border to El Paso, Texas, before my father joined the Army. That’s when we lived in Chicago for a short time, then Colorado and Germany before we briefly returned to Juárez. I was about 13 when we moved to El Paso again.

What places feel like home?

Anywhere I hear the Spanish of the US-Mexico border. These areas are often ignored and underserved so it’s a working-class Spanish. Because of its location, some words are a mix of English and Spanish that other parts of Mexico don’t use. 

Other than family members, who or what has shaped you the most?

The decade between graduating high school and enrolling at El Paso Community College. I spent most of it working in construction and bouncing around between El Paso and Phoenix, along with a few bad months in Tucson. 

What is your favorite time of day?

The early morning when everyone is asleep and the sun’s yet to rise. And it’s so quiet that, almost always at the exact same time, I can hear my neighbor’s footsteps as they walk out of their home, open and close their car door, start it, and then drive away, presumably on their way to work.

What are you really good at?

Building things. I find it almost therapeutic to do some sort of work with my hands as I sweat and listen to music. I also enjoy the feeling of seeing something finished within a few hours. 

What’s the best gift you’ve ever received?

I don’t remember who I got the idea from, but years ago I heard or read a suggestion to interview your children during different phases of their lives. Just take out the voice recorder and ask them basic questions. When they’re younger, you can ask about their favorite animal, color, movie, etc. As they get older, the questions can be more about their friends, hobbies, and aspirations. 

I’ve been doing this every few months with my now 9-year-old daughter. Occasionally, I’ll listen to the first recordings from when she was 3, and I can hear how much she’s changed—from her voice and interests to the clarity of her words and thoughts. It’s like a short visit with a different version of who your child once was.

That suggestion to interview your children has been the best gift.

Describe your favorite meal.

My mom’s pozole. It’s a Mexican pork and hominy stew accompanied with radishes, cabbage, and bolillo bread. She’ll sometimes make it in late October, on the Saturday closest to my birthday. The weather will be colder by then and a college football game will be on in the background—both of those make it even better. Then a good cigar afterwards.

Sound or silence? (And if sound, what sound?)

It’s become silence. I used to write with music in the background. It almost didn’t matter what kind, and sometimes it’d be the same song on repeat for hours. That was also when I’d do most of my writing during the day and into the early evening. But now, I’ve fallen into a routine where I do most of my writing early. Sometimes I’ll wake up naturally as early as three in the morning. With that change, I now write in silence. 

But maybe it’ll change back to music one day.

Where do you do your best thinking?

It just happens so there’s no specific place. And so long as I’m not on deadline, whenever I feel like I can’t think anymore I just try to do something else for that day.

I’ve gotten ideas while driving, listening to podcasts and music, or in the middle of watching a movie. I’ve even woken up during the middle of night with a thought that helps unlock something that I had been stuck on. 

What journey—physical, creative, intellectual, or otherwise—has meant the most to you?

Earning an associate degree. 

I was a nontraditional student who first enrolled at El Paso Community College at 28 years old. It had been about a decade since I was in school. I was full of self-doubt and worry that I was too old or not a good enough student to be there. With that, I also worried that I might be wasting my time. 

But I quickly realized I was a much better student in college than I’d ever been in high school. I was motivated, disciplined, and having worked in construction for the decade before then, I had a different perspective of what college could be. Whenever I felt like complaining, I’d remind myself (as I’ll still occasionally do) that reading and writing is a lot easier than doing manual labor outdoors, especially during the summers. 

I ultimately transferred and graduated from a four-year university, and later even finished a PhD program. But that associate degree was the most meaningful because it’s where I started to find outlets for my intellectual curiosities and people who encouraged me. 

Where do you like to read?

I don’t have any specific place. At home it’s usually in my office, bed, or on the couch. Away from there, I’ll read while waiting. I’m an anxious flyer, so I’ve also recently found myself saving longer reads for when I’m at the airport or on a plane. It lets me focus on something else while also helping pass the time.  

What’s the last rabbit hole you disappeared into?

The World Cup.

Name three publications you enjoy reading these days.

Texas Highways to read about the parts of Texas that aren’t chaotic or depressive. De Los to keep up with some of what’s happening with Latinos outside of where I live. The Good Fight to stay current with boxing.

What’s one longread that you can’t stop thinking about?

Michael Paterniti’s “The House that Thurman Munson Built.” It’s got everything that interests me as a reader and writer: tragedy, memory, and examining what athletes mean to us at different ages.

What was the last book you read?

Divided Soul: The Life of Marvin Gaye. It’s an excellent book. 

What piece of nonfiction are you most proud of writing?

I don’t know if “proud” is the right word for it since it’s such a heartbreaking story. But “‘She made us happy’: The all-star dreams of Uvalde’s biggest José Altuve fan” is the first thing that comes to mind.

What’s your most reliable way to get creatively unstuck?

Go for a walk or drive. Either of those help me get away from what I’m doing without completely separating me from it.

Who’s a writer you turn to when you need some inspiration?

Wright Thompson, who I’m fortunate to call a colleague. 

I’ll sometimes listen to a chapter or two from The Cost of These Dreams on audiobook before I start writing a story. Wright is among the best sports writers ever, but the story of his that I’ll most often return to is the one he wrote for The Atlantic, “His Name Was Emmett Till.” The small part where one of the main characters says he doesn’t think of the past but has a dog named Dixie is perfect.

What words do you overuse?

“Practically,” “essentially,” “actual(ly),” “that,” “even.” 

And in first drafts, I start too many sentences with “so,” “because,” and “since.” 

What’s your favorite guilty pleasure?

Watching mindless, and at times dumb, dating shows with my wife. 

What superpower would you like to have? 

The ability to not get distracted by my phone. 

What animal or nonhuman being do you most identify with?

Stray dogs who largely mind their own business and hang out in the same general area without terrorizing it. 

If you have a free solitary hour in your day, what do you typically do?

If it’s early in the day, I’ll take a nap. 

What five items would you place in a time capsule?

My phone full of photos and videos, a drawing from my daughter, my box full of sports cards, my voice recorder, and a Dallas Cowboys Super Bowl XXX champions hat because I increasingly fear that’ll be the last one they’ll win.

What does your writing space look like?

I’ve turned a room in our house into my office. It has a wall-to-wall bookcase. On the opposite side of it is my desk. It has plenty of space, a filing cabinet attached to it, and a shelf for my speaker and printer. Yes, a printer. It’s nothing fancy, but practical. 

On the wall above the desk is a dry-erase board where I’ll write reminders and a few words that are story ideas. Once those ideas become a story, I have a corkboard, on the wall to the left of where I sit, for the three-by-five cards I use to outline and organize sections. Above the corkboard are reminders of what I need to focus on when I write. Below it is a calendar for deadlines and travel dates. To the right of where I sit is a small couch. The walls have framed boxing fight posters, work of local artists, photos of my wife and daughter, and random things that mean something to me, like mini football helmets from the University of Texas-El Paso. 

Roberto José Andrade Franco is a feature writer with ESPN and a Writer-at-Large with Texas Highways. His work has been anthologized four times in The Year’s Best Sports Writing and nominated for the National Magazine Award. He’s also a four-time finalist for the Dan Jenkins Medal for Excellence in Sportswriting.

title: Until Dawn 2 is notably cheaper than most first-party PlayStation games, but is this anything to be worried about?
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Sun prices aren't rising.

Choice-and-consequence horror game Until Dawn 2, which only just got a release date, has also gone up for pre-ordering on the PlayStation Store. And the revealing bit about this is that the PS5-exclusive title is priced £45 on the UK PS Store (as spotted by Push Square), which makes it a slightly cheaper offering than a full-priced game normally is.

This lower price is notable among the line-up of first-party PlayStation Studios games. This year's Saros was priced £70 / $70, and Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls was £60 / $60. And later this month, Marvel's Wolverine is £70 / $70 again.

It's a pleasing discovery, although it does beg the question of "why?". Could the price signify a shorter adventure than we're typically used to?

Until Dawn 2 trades the snowy lodge environment of the first game for a tropical resort called Akishima Island, and stars an entirely new cast of characters, albeit with one exception - the recurring Peter Stormare character of Dr. Hill.

The sequel is not developed by the original's Supermassive Games, incidentally. Instead, it's helmed by Firesprite Games, with some help from Dispatch developer AdHoc Studio.

The original Until Dawn celebrated its 10th anniversary last year. We spoke to creative director Will Byles about how the game set a new standard for cinematic horror storytelling in games. In the same interview, Byles recalled how Sony pulled all marketing at the last minute after not liking the game.

Until Dawn 2 is set for release on 28th January on PS5.

title: Solarpunk MMO Loftia is launching into early access November 3
author: Issy van der Velde
content:
Loftia early access launch date reveal trailer - PC Gaming Show 2026 - YouTube

Watch On

How come the future in videogames is, more often than not, dark and gloomy? Where's the hope? Where's the optimism? It's all in Loftia, an MMO life sim with a delightfully cheery, eco-friendly aesthetic. And, as was just revealed at the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct, you'll be able to get your hands on it November 3.

For those of you not in the know, Loftia is an eco-optimism life sim MMO that's been in development for the last four years. You and other players inhabiting the world will each get your own floating island to call home, and you've got a bunch of sustainable ways to decorate and power your slice of sanctuary.

Wishlist Loftia on Steam

Early access release date: November 3, 2026

Build a sustainable home on a sky island and work with your community to build the third space of your dreams. Wishlist Loftia on Steam.

Wishlist now

You can grow crops in cute hydroponic shelves, rescue animals, and go on adventures with other people. These aren't focused on combat, and will instead feature puzzles and platforming challenges. There are also community projects that everyone can join in on, so you can live out your commune dreams.

"We wanted a relaxing online world we could escape to with our friends—a third space with a welcoming community, things to do, and a home we could keep on coming back to." said Michael Su, co-founder and studio director of Qloud Games.

In the new trailer, we see a lot of the customisation on offer in Loftia. From your avatar, to your pets, to your home in the clouds, you can decorate pretty much everything. It also hints at the main point of friction that will be driving you forwards. Some world-ending event is coming, causing literal cracks in the sky islands, and it'll be down to you and everyone else to come together and figure out how to save your community.

Loftia launches into early access November 3, 2026. You can wishlist it on Steam.

Check out our Steam page with all the games, updates, and DLC featured in the show. You can also read our roundup article which includes every announcement from the show in the order it aired.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Issy van der Velde has been writing about video games professionally for five years, contributing to Rolling Stone, NME, GamesRadar+, IGN, and many more. He's been freelance and held editorial roles across news, guides, and features, and is now the deputy editor of the PC Gaming Show.

A lifelong gamer, Issy won the MCV 30 under 30 award for his work covering queer, Arab, and women's representation in the gaming industry.

His favourite games are narrative, story-driven adventures, arcade racers, roguelites, and soulslikes.

title: After two weeks with Steam Frame, Valve's latest is now my go-to VR headset, but my recommendation comes with some important caveats
author: @eurogamer
content:
And so here it is: Steam Frame; Valve's second in-house VR headset following 2019's Index, featuring a boosted spec sheet, PC-to-headset streaming, and the ability to function standalone. It is, if you don't mind spoilers, a good, often great bit of kit, and a fascinating machine - it's lightweight and wonderfully comfortable, with some neat ideas, and it's a pleasure to use if you're doing PC-to-VR. As a standalone device, though, I have reservations, and there's a sense that it's perhaps not quite ready for prime time.

Before we get too far into things, though, a caveat: I love VR, I think it's cool in its niche, and capable of offering a uniquely immersive way to enjoy games (Fireproof's wonderful urban fantasy adventure Ghost Town and Studio Chyr's properly discombobulating room-scale puzzler Hotel Infinity are unquestionably two of my favourite releases of last year). But I'm definitely more of a casual VR fan and not especially technically minded, so if it's a thorough tech breakdown and analysis you're after, Will Judd's Steam Frame preview from last year is a good place to start, followed by RPS hardware editor James Archer's Steam Frame review.

What I can do, though, is whizz through the basics. And compared to Valve's previous foray into VR, 2019's Index, Steam Frame is a huge step up in every way. Its weight has been almost halved, down to 440g from 800g; its screen resolution has been boosted from 1440x1600 per eye to 2160x2160; its display runs between 72Hz and 144Hz, and gone are the old fresnel lenses in favour of pancake lenses, enabling thinner headsets and increased clarity. Movement and position tracking is now handled by on-device cameras rather than separate base stations situated around the room; Frame has an on-device battery so it can be used without being connected to the mains, and, of course, it can operate standalone.

In terms of more modern comparisons, Frame isn't quite as radical an upgrade from 2023's Meta Quest 3 - still one of the most popular consumer VR headsets and a machine I'm more intimately familiar with - but it absolutely brings notable improvements. Per-eye screen resolution is slightly higher than Quest 3's 2064x2208 (but unlike Sony's PSVR2, neither headset features OLED panels), it's slightly lighter (Quest 3 weighs 515g), and it features in-device eyetracking. Elsewhere, Frame contains twice as much internal memory (16GB versus Quest 3's 8GB), and a more performative CPU: the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 versus Quest 3's Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 - which should, says RPS' James Archer, be around 30 percent more powerful in synthetic terms, providing a performance advantage over Quest given Frame only has about two percent more pixels to push.

So what does all this technology cost? Well, Steam Frame isn't cheap. It starts at £889 for the 256GB model - £340 more than the popular Meta Quest 3, which has 512GB of storage - and climbs to £1,089 if you want 1TB. For that, you get the headset and a swappable battery pack that lives round the back of your head, two controllers, a USB streaming dongle, a charging cable, and a spacer for your glasses - although Valve partner Zenni Optical is offering snap-in prescription lenses for around $70 a pair. Then there are the optional upgrades: the £59 Ergonomic Accessories Kit and the separate £29 PSU if you need one.

For some, the £340+ difference between Quest 3 and Frame (likely a result of the AI-fuelled component crisis driving up hardware costs, the better bits inside the Frame, and the fact that, unlike Meta, Valve doesn't subsidise its hardware) won't be factor, particularly if it means they can avoid Meta's Faustian Pact. For others it'll be a far more significant consideration. But whatever you make of the price, my two weeks messing around with Steam Frame have revealed a good bit of hardware with the potential to be great.

Set-up, as you'd hope, is all very simple, aside from an unexpected 40-minute halt as the headset installed its first update - although it's unclear if that's to be expected or just a quirk of the pre-release beta software. And once that's sorted, a number of options immediately present themselves: you can install your games directly to Frame's internal storage for standalone play (Frame supports VR games and flatscreen games via Valve's Proton compatibility layer), or you can stream directly from your PC.

Valve, if you weren't aware, is leaning heavily into Frame's ability to play flatscreen games, which makes a lot of sense: both as a unique selling point, and given the current VR climate, which has seen a slowing of VR-focused game releases. And to handle potential compatibility issues, it's implemented a Steam Frame verification system similar to its work with Steam Deck and Steam Machine, meaning everything listed as 'Great on Frame' in your Steam library and in-store should run well in standalone mode. Valve says around 130 games will be Steam Frame verified at launch, but that figure is split between VR games and traditional flatscreen titles (the latter must hit 720p at 30fps and the former must "run at a minimum of 72 fps at 1728x1728" to meet Valve's verification requirements).

And the first big surprise for me after firing Frame up was just how few of the VR games I own currently have Valve's 'verified' seal of approval: Arizona Sunshine 2, Pistol Whip, Moss VR, The Room VR, and Walkabout Golf (my non-VR verified list was far more expansive, including the likes of Factorio, Dread, Inside, Animal Well, Dave the Diver, Silksong, Portal 2, and Streets of Rage 4). Any excuse to play Walkabout Golf is a good excuse in my book, however, and, as expected, its cheery low-poly golfing runs flawlessly in Frame's standalone mode. And the lack of faff required to get it running smoothly provided a handily consistent baseline for testing as I started to get to grips with the Steam Frame hardware itself.

And where better to begin than the headset? There's obviously no getting around the fact you've still got a not-insubstantial bit of hardware clamped around your head - it's the fundamental limitation of VR - but Steam Frame is undoubtedly the most comfortable VR headset I've tried yet. In comparison, the front-heavy Quest 3 feels like a brick. It's light (the front core is apparently just 185g) and extremely well-balanced; by clamping the battery pack to the rear of your head, weight is shifted from the goggles and spread more evenly around your dome, making it more manageable for longer play sessions. But gravity is gravity, and, in its out-of-the-box configuration, that 400g did eventually attempt to return to earth, creating familiar forehead discomfort as it slowly slid its way down my face. Which is where Valve's optional Accessories Kit began to feel like an essential purchase.

This includes controller grip straps (snugger and more secure than the default Switch-style wrist bands, and enabling you to hold the controllers open-palmed in lieu of handtracking), a sort of rubbery nose flap, and most importantly, a headstrap which provides additional support for Steam Frame, shifting some of its weight from your face. With it installed, I found I could play far longer using the headset, even if it does introduce a few quirks. Chiefly, the strap pulls the top of the headset inward, creating a gap for light to creep in toward the bottom of the goggles, which is where the nose flap comes in. Fitting it is a fascinating adventure, requiring you to pretty much pull the entire headset apart using its clasps and clips - a simple process that provides insight into just how elegantly modular the device is - but once it was in, I did find quite a lot of light could still creep in from below.

As for the headset's picture quality, it's crisp and decently rich, but not, to my eyes at least, an especially notable step up from Quest 3 (I've not used the OLED PSVR2 to compare). It's still quite a 'goggly' headset, too, despite its "up to 110 degrees" field of view. And audio is a touch underwhelming. It utilises "dual speaker drivers per ear, integrated into headstrap", and they're punchy enough, capable of conveying a convincing surround soundscape, but bass leaves something to be desired. And while there's no headphone jack, one of my interviews with Valve mentioned an "enthusiast" accessories pack coming a few months after launch, supposedly including a "premium" audio solution, alongside a swappable battery (right now, you'll get an hour or so of play in standalone mode on a single charge, which isn't great).

Any other quirks? Steam Frame's fan vents circulate a notable amount of cool air around your eyeballs, and eject a surprisingly amount of heat out top - but it's angled in a way that so far hasn't been a concern. Also, I've found it a little tricky to adjust the headset when it's on my face without accidentally dislodging the magnetised strip that holds its cushioning foam in place, requiring a bit of fishing around to recover it. But this stuff is mildly irksome at best, and it's still an extremely comfortable headset I've enjoyed a lot.

One other thing that's worth mentioning: Frame's passthrough cameras, which allow you to see the world outside your headset, are monochrome. Personally, I haven't missed the downgrade from Quest's full-colour cameras given I generally only use pass-through for outside orientation, but if you're a fan of mixed reality gaming it might be a concern. Valve partner Arcturus has, however, created a full-colour camera upgrade for £129/€157/$149, which it claims offers fidelity "beyond" Quest 3 and Apple Vision Pro.

As for Steam Frame's controllers, they're also good! Each weighs around 140g, supports six degrees of rotational freedom, plus full finger and thumb tracking, and you should get around 40 hours on a pair of AA batteries. During play, they feel precise and responsive, and ergonomically, they're very similar to Quest 3's Touch Plus controllers, meaning they sit comfortably and naturally in my average-sized hands, and are lightweight without feeling insubstantial. Notably, though, Frame includes a more generous series of inputs compared to Meta's offering: there's a d-pad on the left controller and four face buttons on the right; each has a control stick, a clicky shoulder button and more resistant trigger beneath it, plus a "dual-stage" inner grip trigger that, if I'm honest, feels a touch too flimsy for my tastes.

But the important bit here: by mirroring the layout of a standard gamepad, pretty much every Proton-compatible flatscreen title you care to throw at Frame should work just fine natively using the included controllers (although you can connect other gamepads, mice, and keyboards via bluetooth if you like). And, actually, I've quite enjoyed Frame's cinema-like wraparound experience while tootling through Cuphead and Hades in standalone mode - and given Frame supports Steam features like cloud saves, it's an easy hop between devices. A minor moan: I'm not a huge fan of the vast circular void Valve still insists on using as a VR backdrop (a couple of cosier options would be nice for flatscreen play), but it does have a few neat tricks. You can, for instance, set the surrounding virtual uplights to mirror what's happening in-game, adding a cute bit of extra immersion while playing.

There's a bit of an important caveat to all this flatscreen talk, though. As nice a feature as it is, especially when there's no guarantee of a regular release cadence for new VR games, Steam Frame isn't a processing powerhouse (it isn't even as powerful as Steam Deck, RPS' James Archer informs me), and that's going to limit what you can play in standalone mode. After a bit of experimentation, 2D games, even those still unverified, seem reliably playable as long as they're supported by Valve's Proton compatibility layer (which essentially allows your Windows games to work on the headset's Linux-based operating system). But when I moved onto modest 3D indies that didn't have Valve's tick, the results were variable. Games like Botany Garden failed to sustain a stable framerate, even on its lowest settings, suggesting most modern blockbusters are out the window unless their dev teams want to roll up sleeves and optimise specifically for Frame. Older-era titles like Dark Souls 2 should work, but even so, I found playing 3D games at 30fps in VR unpleasant enough that I'll likely stick to 2D.

My bigger issue, though, is Frame's standalone VR experience, which feels a little too hit and miss right now. Frame's Proton compatibility layer does a good job of actually getting your games to open, but the results are unpredictable, especially given how comparatively few VR titles are currently verified. Some games I tried work flawlessly out of the box (Walkabout Golf, The Room VR, Pistol Whip, Arizona Sunshine 2), some work well enough with minimal tinkering (Tetris Effect, Ghost Town), others didn't work at all (Serious Sam VR and Escape Simulator refused to boot, The Walking Dead: Saints & Sinners got stuck on the menu, and Myst VR crashed so hard it turned my headset off). Others are absolute slideshows, even on their lowest settings (not that I was expecting much success with No Man's Sky given Frame's standalone limitations), and others are technically playable, but only if you're willing to ditch antialiasing and opt for the lowest resolution.

There's just a little bit too much faff as a standalone experience, and the end results too often feel slightly compromised - it's certainly far removed from the slick plug-and-play of Meta's native games library. Of course, if developers are able to properly optimise their games for the Frame and get that verification tick, the problem should ease with time. But, even so, I can't help feeling verification should be further along than it is right now.

As for the Frame version of Half-Life: Alyx - a game worth mentioning given that it's free with all purchases, and has, according to Valve, shaped so much of Frame's hardware - it's an impressive achievement, making zero concessions in terms of gameplay. Alyx's wonderfully unpredictable mix of blockbuster action and horror, its slick cinematic pacing and clever immersive tricks, still makes for an incredible experience. But there are some compromises you'll have to reckon with. And I found the swirling, shimmering jaggies constantly on the edge of my peripheral vision (it uses foveated rendering to dynamically increase the resolution of whatever you're looking at) just a little too intrusive and distracting.

But! The PC-to-headset experience Valve has cooked up for Frame is a delight, and perhaps the most compelling reason - for me at least - to make the switch from Quest. It all works through Frame's bundled-in dongle, officially a "plug and play 6GHz wireless adapter", that provides an entirely wirefree way of streaming your VR and non-VR games from your PC (but not Steam Machine, at present) to your headset. As someone who has routinely managed to tangle themselves into a wire-based PC-to-VR deathgrip in the past, and who has utterly failed to get Meta's wi-fi reliant Air Link feature working, Valve's solution is elegant and effortless enough to be, for my needs at least, a game changer.

From a tech perspective, as far as I understand at least, the key to it all is foveated streaming - which, in a similar fashion to foveated rendering, uses your eye position to optimise network bandwidth and image quality by decreasing bitrate and pixels outside where you're looking at. And to my eyes, it works extremely well, letting me use the extra grunt of my PC - summoning the added visual bells and whistles, the higher resolution, and refresh rates - while being wire-free, faff-free, and with no obvious degradation in image quality or latency. It's got good range too: I successfully managed to stream to the more room-scale-VR-appropriate office across the hallway from my computer, but your mileage may vary if you don't live in a new-build with paper-thin walls. In fact, the only time the dongle failed was when I ramped up all No Man's Sky's settings, pushing my PC too hard and taking streaming with it.

So that's the Steam Frame. As a standalone machine, I have some reservations: it can be fiddly and unpredictable, far from the plug-and-play ease of Meta Quest, but that's an issue Valve's expanding verification programme will hopefully address over time. But as a PC-to-VR device, it's a delight; liberating in its stress-free, wire-free functionality, if you can deal with the fleeting battery life. And that - alongside the feature bump and wonderfully comfortable headset - has already made Frame my go-to headset, Quest exclusives aside. Frame isn't a machine for high-end enthusiasts though, I don't think, and despite its many nice-to-haves, it perhaps doesn't offer a dramatically different in-headset experience to the far cheaper, more intuitive Quest 3, meaning Meta's machine is still in the conversation. And so, honestly, I'm not sure if the Frame is for you. But as unhelpful as this might be, if you think it is, you're probably right.

A Steam Frame was provided for this review by Valve.

title: Rockstar asks modders to please take its games very seriously
author: Lincoln Carpenter
content:
What happened

  • On September 10, Rockstar Games published new mod guidelines on its website, which it says are intended to "maintain a fun, creative, and welcoming place for players and content creators."
  • The guidelines are seem primarily targeted at mods for the FiveM and RedM platforms, which Rockstar acquired—along with their developers—in 2023.
  • Rockstar says mods must "respect our games": As part of its "right to set limits on how others can use our games and brand," the studio says mods can't expand or modify official storylines, missions, and characters, and can't combine settings and characters from different Rockstar franchises.
  • Rockstar says modders can't incorporate other intellectual property or real-world likenesses, and forbids cheat menus or modifications that interfere with its official multiplayer and online services.
  • Rockstar calls its official modding platforms "the exclusive licensed home for our community to monetize their mods," forbidding alternative monetization or commercialization of mods for its games.

Do these guidelines have any teeth?

Like Rockstar's more formal terms of service and platform license agreements, these guidelines are the sort of standard rhetorical armament a company equips itself with when in case it needs a quick fix for something egregious: If a mod emerges that could give the studio a legal or financial headache, all it'll need to do is tap the sign before giving the offending user-generated content the boot.

Of course, those guidelines are theoretically more difficult to enforce on platforms the studio doesn't own. For Rockstar, removing a mod that breaks its commandments is easy enough on FiveM. But if that mod's on a third party site—like the one our Josh Wolens used to murder a charmander on the streets of Los Santos—making that problem go away isn't so simple. House rules are a lot harder to enforce at someone else's house.

That hasn't stopped Rockstar in the past, however: In 2021, it sent takedown notices to a number of modding projects that reverse-engineered, restored, or reimplemented elements of older GTA games. It announced and released its trio of GTA Trilogy remasters later that year.

title: Where Cities and Oceans Meet
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
What does it mean to live in a disappearing place? For Pioneer Works’ Broadcast, Brad Bolman, a professor of history and environmental studies at Tulane University, writes about New Orleans, the shifting borders between land and sea, and the political and economic forces that continue to shape the city’s fate in a time of climate catastrophe.

If Los Angeles is the city that has been imaginatively destroyed again and again in film and TV, as Thom Andersen argues in Los Angeles Plays Itself, New Orleans is the one that has been destroyed countless times in reality. We have survived worse and rebuilt before, many insisted. We’re staying.

It was a reaction as understandable emotionally as it was disconnected from environmental reality. But that gap is a feature of life in the Crescent City. As I watched my first Mardi Gras parade this spring, junk falling in never-ending torrents from brightly decorated floats, a friend sympathetically interjected, “This must be driving you crazy.” What they meant was that as someone who teaches about environmental history but isn’t from here, I must be especially affected by the throwaway culture of the city’s most famous fête and its tons and tons of plastic beads, made from the same fossil fuels that are causing sea levels to rise around us.

title: Even Ed Sheeran’s Apology Took Both Sides
author: @NewYorker
content:
One of Ed Sheeran’s enduring contributions to the texture of twenty-first-century music—let’s say you are looking for one—will probably be the repopularization of the loop pedal. This is a technology, which Sheeran mastered in his early years as a busker, that lets a guy perform with himself, in echoes, alone, harmonizing with his own voice. The loop pedal allows the bedroom beat-maker and the YouTube singer to go out into the real world. It can turn an acoustic guitar into a threat. On his current world tour, Sheeran has spent a lot of time standing and looping alone. Ahead of his most recent performance, in Philadelphia, he had allowed one of his supporting acts, the rapper Macklemore, to be removed from the tour for saying the words “Free Palestine” onstage. Sheeran’s remaining supporting acts—the band Lukas Graham and the singer-songwriters Aaron Rowe and Finneas—and his backing band, the Irish folk troupe Beoga, all withdrew in solidarity.

The musical contributions of Macklemore have been fewer than Sheeran’s, yet morally clearer. At two previous concerts, in New Jersey, the Seattle-based rapper had performed his protest song “Hind’s Hall,” named after a building that protesters at Columbia had renamed for Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl who had been killed by Israeli soldiers. I had been orbiting the political side of Macklemore for some time—in 2017, he caused a similar news event by performing the anti-homophobia song “Same Love” at a high-profile sporting event in Australia during a gay-marriage vote, which I covered—and, over the years, I’d become warily appreciative of the rapper, best known, previously, for novelty songs and his earnest-white-boy persona.

In the lead-up to the concert in Philadelphia, social media had been flooded with mirror images of the same joke: “I’m trying to separate the art from the artist but the other way around,” of Macklemore; “I’m trying to think of a way to boycott Ed Sheeran’s music more than I usually do,” for Sheeran. It felt nice, for a while, to add to Sheeran and Macklemore two things that, respectively, they lack: politics and relevance.

Recently, the most exciting thing about Sheeran seemed to be his cowardice. A few hours before the show, a hundred or so local protesters gathered at a nearby train station. The demonstrators seemed embarrassed by the fact that they had been brought there by an Ed Sheeran concert. “Thank you for being here today for what I would like to be known as a show of support for Gaza and uplifting voices in Palestine, and not the ‘Ed Sheeran rally,’ ” an organizer in a blue shirt said into a megaphone. (A man named Mack told me that the focus should remain on Gaza, and he pointed out that tank shells used in the attack that killed Hind Rajab had been made by a Philadelphia-based weapons company, Day & Zimmermann.)

A protester named Asa Khalif, who wore a shirt that said “STOP GENOCIDE,” described Sheeran’s music as “beige and bland,” adding, “For those who are in love and want to have a wedding song—so be it.” He had a higher opinion of Macklemore: “ ‘Thrift Shop,’ I think, was genius. And it’s stood the test of time.” Another attendee told me, “I wouldn’t say I’m a fan of Macklemore, but I like what he does.”

How did the Sheeran fans feel? Outside the concert venue, a woman wearing a Taylor Swift shirt (she told me that she’s liked Sheeran ever since his appearance on Swift’s song “Everything Has Changed,” and “because he looks like Ron Weasley”) said that she was disappointed in Sheeran, but “sometimes singers can’t do anything.” (Reportedly, Sheeran had been asked to drop Macklemore by Robert Kraft, who owns the stadium in Boston that Sheeran is set to perform at next; Sheeran has said that the decision to remove Macklemore was made by the tour promoter.) The woman said that Sheeran had experienced his own troubles. “After his wife’s cancer battle, this might just be too much for him,” she said. “He’s, like, ‘Can’t we have one night of peace, every time I go do a concert, and not think about stuff?’ ”

“I’m in agreement with Macklemore,” Rachealle Davis, a Sheeran fan from Scotland, said. Of Sheeran, she added, “I think maybe he should have grown a set of balls.” Still, an Ed Sheeran concert is a form of “escapism,” she said. “It’s easy listening. We’ve listened to it most of our life.” Two mega-fans, Eva Stevens and Kizzy Holton, wearing Sheeran tour shirts, had driven up from Maryland. “I think Ed is apolitical, period,” Holton said, approvingly. “I think that he kind of sits in the middle of all the issues.”

It has, arguably, never been more pop to be political. More than two thousand miles away and three weeks earlier, Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival, hosted by Olivia Rodrigo, had politics as its purpose. Hayley Williams, the lead singer of Paramore, recently interpolated the lines “Fuck ICE” and “Free Palestine” into a song, during a live performance. Stevens said the middle was now the most dangerous place to be. “Those are the people who get picked on,” she said.

I brought up Rodrigo and suggested that Sheeran, in his attempts to stay neutral, now seemed to be the outlier. “But you know what?” Stevens said, “That takes heart.” Holton agreed. We were standing near the stadium; a beautiful sunset was coming down over the parking lot. Holton said, “It takes courage to stand alone in the gap.”

I was curious to see how a concert with no opener would open. Now that the event was Mackle-less, ticket prices had dropped dramatically, but the stadium was fairly full. (I found a scarcely believable survey, conducted by the British phone company O2, that ranked Sheeran as the third artist that respondents were most interested in seeing live, after the Beatles and Queen.) Around me, in the nosebleeds, were a mix of children in big friend groups and softly bopping couples. The pre-show screen displayed a graphic of a peaceful, undulating pink wave.

Sheeran emerged—alone, in jeans and a blue T-shirt—to a huge cheer, and began with an apology. Reading partly from a teleprompter, he said he’d been “making mistakes” over the past week—he did not mention the names of any of his former supporting acts—and added, “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable.”

“Everyone here can stand beside people they don’t agree with on everything, but they can all agree on singing these songs,” he said, then strummed his guitar into “Castle on the Hill,” a frenetic, bass-drum-heavy track about being homesick and fulfilling your dreams. Fireworks shot up from the stage. (Usually, Sheeran starts each show on the tour with a song called “You Need Me, I Don’t Need You.” Not this time.)

The stage for Sheeran’s tour has a glittering circular screen set into its center, twinkling like a ring light. It reminded me of the Portal, the short-lived art installation in New York that allowed people to wave at—or, in some instances, flash—people at a matching screen, in Dublin. For the two nights that Macklemore had performed on the tour, he had used the screen to display images of destruction in Gaza, as though it were a grim magic mirror. Sheeran often used it to show his feet as they hit the loop pedals.

I had been waiting to see what would happen when Sheeran arrived at the middle segment of his show, which he usually plays with the Irish band Beoga. Before “Galway Girl,” a Sheeran song for which Beoga’s violinist, Niamh Dunne, had written the main riff, Sheeran announced that he had replaced them. “When my friends dropped out of this show,” he explained, he had turned to Alicia Enstrom, a violinist from Kansas, and a crew of stand-ins, who, Sheeran told us, repeatedly, had learned Beoga’s parts in three days. (He did not mention Beoga by name.) As they played “Galway Girl,” the screen displayed an Irish knot and flashed the colors of the Irish flag, while green-and-red fireworks went off.

Sheeran repeatedly said that his shows brought people together, and it was charming to see groups of friends, mostly young, turning and singing to one another. (I also enjoyed “Thinking Out Loud.”) But, for all the talk of Sheeran as easy listening and harmonious, I found the listening not so easy. In between songs, he kept talking about how this had been the worst week of his life, in a tone of self-pity. “How am I going to get musicians to stand onstage with me,” he asked, “in a week where no one wants to stand onstage with me?” Sheeran said that he had removed a B-stage—one that extends into the audience—because he was “afraid of what might happen.” At one point, he sat cross-legged and said that he wondered whether he “even wanted to be an artist at all.”

But everyone else seemed happy to be there, and cheered each message of neutrality. There was a moment, during the scripted mea culpa, when the crowd roared after Sheeran said that he wanted his shows to be about “humanity, not politics,” cutting him off before he could say, “But this is a humanitarian issue.” It reminded me, slightly, of a tweet that I’d previously thought of as a heightened piece of satire: “Just got back from the centrist rally. Amazing turnout. Thousands of people holding hands and chanting ‘Better things aren’t possible.’ ”

Sheeran said, in as many words, that he was glad nobody there was mad at him. It felt a little enabling. “I’m feeling all of my friends and family abandon me,” he said. “But I look at the end of the week and I see fifty thousand people who haven’t abandoned me.” He added, “I love you.”

The sense of atonement faded as the night went on. Toward the end of the show, Sheeran told the crowd, “The one thing that I would like to apologize for is the first bit of the show where it wasn’t about music, and I had to talk”—the apology. In the past twenty-four hours, other artists, including Jack Antonoff and Imagine Dragons, had said “Free Palestine” or appeared with a Palestinian flag, onstage. But, if Sheeran’s music is feel-good, then two and a half hours of Ed Sheeran had certainly made the artist feel better. He went offstage and returned in a bright-pink jersey of his favorite soccer team, Ipswich Town, with the name of the tour, Loop, in place of the team sponsor. The stadium staff readied more fireworks. The first song of the encore was “You Need Me, I Don’t Need You.” ♦

title: PlayStation reportedly dumped Hideo Kojima spy action game Physint over exceeded budgets, missed deadlines, and Death Stranding sales
author: Mark Warren
content:
Their enthusiasm physlled out

Earlier this week, Hideo Kojima-helmed action espionage game Physint switched publishers from PlayStation to Xbox, a leap across the console divide which might make it more likely to get a PC port. At the time, Kojima claimed PlayStation had tried to can the game, while the console makers tried to paint the divorce as an amicable split. Now, a report's shed more light on why Sony decided to ditch Physint.

According to the Bloomberg report, the answer is basically every reason you might think a cash-obsessed behemoth still reeling from a bunch of missed live service shots over the past few years would have to get cold feet. Apparently, both Death Stranding and Death Stranding 2 having failed to generate as much revenue as PlayStation hoped played a major role, but that general fear that Kojima games might not be the sort of money printing machines Sony envisioned wasn't the be all and end all.

Kojima Productions had reportedly missed deadlines on Physint, with PlayStation having gotten stricter about production milestones following the likes of Concord's quick demise, and the game was set to be well over budget while still years away from coming out. Also an alleged bugbear was the fact a permanent PlayStation exclusive wasn't waiting at the finish line, contributing to Sony's unwillingness to further open their purse strings for Kojima and co.

All in all, the list of sticking points are exactly the sort of justifications you'd expect to hear from a company probably slightly perturbed that in getting out of a union they weren't happy with, they've ended up handing their most famous competitor an easy PR win. It's arguably an indicator just how far up shit creek the games industry is in 2026 that the chance to boast about having a Kojima game in your catalogue and/or stand next to the auteur at one or more of the year's many showcases no longer seems to offset some or all of the niggling number concerns in the minds of every exec.

When even larger-than-life household names with well-established game-making reputations that big companies love to use to embellish their own are being hot potatoed around, what chance do studios without that in their locker have?

title: Next major Halo game being developed by Activision, as Halo Studios all but closes as part of Microsoft's Xbox restructuring
author: Robert Purchese
content:
A "purpose-built" team separate to Call of Duty will handle it.

Halo Studios (formerly 343 Industries) won't develop the next mainline Halo game because it's being what sounds like drastically reduced in size. Microsoft has instead given development duty to Activision, which is making "a new purpose-built team" separate to Call of Duty to make it.

"We are eliminating 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer," Xbox Studios boss Matt Booty wrote in a statement. "Activision will also be developing the next Halo title, led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market," Booty wrote.

In a statement provided to Kotaku, Activision president Rob Kostich said: "We're thrilled to welcome Halo, Rare, and World's Edge to Activision." (Rare is also going to Activision.) "It's an honor and a responsibility that we do not take lightly. These teams and their games have inspired fans around the world for decades.

"For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place. It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community."

The news arrives as part of another wave of major Microsoft Xbox restructuring, which has seen hundreds more people lose their jobs, British studio Ninja Theory close, and studios like Obsidian and Rare, as mentioned, consolidated into being controlled by others.

The Halo series, originated by Bungie, was overseen by 343 Industries/Halo Studios ever since Bungie bought its independence from Microsoft in 2007. Halo Studios (it rebranded in 2024) made a number of mainline Halo games, including 2012's Halo 4, 2015's Halo 5: Guardians, 2021's Halo Infinite, and most recently the reboot of Halo 1, Halo: Campaign Evolved.

Halo Studios also collaborated on every other Halo project, including 2014's Halo: The Master Chief Collection and the Halo Wars games. This move by Microsoft is, then, a significant departure for the Halo series.

title: 'The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure' walkthrough in Fire Emblem Fortune's Weave
author: @FionnTheBrave
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Sep 22, 2026, 4:27 PM EDT

Fame and fortune don't await you, but you get some nice stuff anyway

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave's "The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure" quest is, at a glance, the ideal quest. You can stay in Dagsion to complete it, and you get a decent bit of money and renown when you do. Depending on where you travel in the city and how much you take in the sights, though, there's a chance you'll have no clue where to look for this little scavenger hunt.

Below, we show you how to clear "The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure" in Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave.

'The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure' walkthrough in Fire Emblem Fortune's Weave

The quest giver has a little scrap of a riddle to help guide you. "A colossus gazes upon Baal's waters. On the stone where she points, something worthy of note." Way back when you start someone's Act 1, Seteth's narration tells you the lake surrounding Dagsion is called Lake Baal, so that's the first clue. You're hunting for something overlooking the lake, which means the port in Lowtown is the best place to go.

Happily, there's just one statue in Lowtown, just east of the Vandahl Trading Company. She's pointing east-ish, but there's no item or treasure trove or anything in sight other than a wall. That's because the treasure is on the other side of the wall, along the little path that takes you down to the harbor side.

Grab it, head back to the quest giver, and you'll get your reward: a Morfis Almanac book, 5,000 gold, and 80 renown. The book is an uncommon one, so it's a very good gift for book lovers and decent for those who prefer uncommon and rare items, like Talimun and Catania.

If you're new to Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, we can help you navigate the complex paths of causality. We have put together explainers on which character you should pick first, how to change heroes, and if you should play in casual or classic mode, so you can set up the campaign according to your preferences.

Fortune's Weave is a massive game, that's why we explain how long it will take for you to finish it. As you progress through the initial Heroic Games matches, you should focus on recruiting more characters, unlocking Boons of Salvation, and spending free time in the best way possible. Just don't forget to visit the Perch and have a quick Bird Time session.
